source_title: Counterfactual Evaluation for Blind Attack Detection in LLM-based Evaluation Systems
baselines_compared: Standard Evaluation (SE) alone serves as the baseline/control condition against which the proposed SE+CFE framework is compared, across all seven LLMs and six datasets
key_result: Under Standard Evaluation (SE) alone, blind-attack submissions (a reworded restatement of the question in place of an answer) achieve attack success rates of 61.8% (GPT-3.5-turbo), 98.2% (GPT-4o-mini), 95.8% (GPT-4o), and 99.8% (o1); adding Counterfactual Evaluation (SE+CFE) raises attack-detection F1 to 97.8%, 95.8%, and 99.8% for GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, and o1 respectively (accuracy >96% for all three), while GPT-3.5-turbo improves more modestly (correct-detection F1 70.8%->82.8%, attack-detection F1 only 0.564); among open-source models, Gemma-12B reaches 89.3% accuracy under SE+CFE while LLaMA-8B underperforms.
technical_summary: Formalizes 'blind attacks' against LLM-based evaluation systems, where a submitted candidate answer is crafted independently of the true answer (e.g., a reworded restatement of the question) to deceive an LLM judge into accepting it regardless of correctness. Proposes a defense framework combining Standard Evaluation (SE) with Counterfactual Evaluation (CFE), which re-runs the evaluation against a deliberately substituted false ground-truth answer; an attack is flagged when the submission is validated under both the true and the counterfactual ground truth, since blind attacks are invariant to this substitution while honest answers are not. Evaluates across six QA datasets and seven LLMs (four proprietary, three open-source), showing standard evaluation is highly vulnerable (attack success rates up to 99.8%) while SE+CFE substantially improves attack detection (F1 up to 99.8%) with minimal loss in benign-case accuracy, though weaker models like GPT-3.5-turbo and LLaMA-8B benefit less.
datasets_benchmarks: Six English QA datasets sampled at 100 questions each (600 total): GSM8K, HotpotQA, SQuAD 1.1, StrategyQA, TriviaQA, TruthfulQA

source_title: PromptGuard a structured framework for injection resilient language models
baselines_compared: Internal ablations and component baselines only: regex-only detection, MiniBERT-only detection, flat (unstructured) prompts, and a no-detection baseline; layer-wise ablations isolate Layers 1 and 3. Prior defenses (InjectGuard, PromptFuzz, HonestLLM, JATMO) are compared in a literature table, not run empirically.
key_result: PromptGuard reduces injection success rate by up to 67% across GPT-4, Claude 3 and LLaMA 2 and reaches F1 0.91 for detection with under 8% added latency. The hybrid regex+MiniBERT detector beats regex-only (F1 0.75) and BERT-only (F1 0.86); structured ChatML/JSON prompts alone cut ISR by 40-44% versus flat concatenated prompts; the full pipeline leaves a residual ISR of 14.3% under dynamic multi-turn injection.
technical_summary: Proposes PromptGuard, a modular four-layer, retraining-free defense pipeline against prompt injection: (1) input gatekeeping combining regex pattern matching with a fine-tuned MiniBERT intent classifier, (2) structured prompt formatting using role-tagged ChatML/JSON to prevent semantic blending of system and user content, (3) semantic output validation by a secondary LLM-as-Critic, and (4) Adaptive Response Refinement that rewrites flagged outputs. Evaluates each layer against a matched public dataset and reports ISR, F1, semantic alignment and ROUGE-L/BLEU across three black-box LLMs. Demonstrates that the layers are complementary, with regex filtering cheap explicit cases and offloading 45% of classifier work. The comparison is against its own ablated configurations rather than against re-run prior defenses.
datasets_benchmarks: PromptBench (microsoft/promptbench, used for RQ2 structured-formatting evaluation); Kaggle 'prompt-injection-malignant' (RQ1 input detection; abstract instead names InjectBench); TruthfulQA (817 items, RQ3 output validation); UDora-RedTest adversarial samples for the Layer-3 ablation

source_title: Adaptive Multi‑Layer Framework for Detecting and Mitigating Prompt Injection Attacks in Large Language Models
baselines_compared: Internal ablations only - five configurations (no defense, CAP only, OV only, CAP+OV, CAP+OV+SFL). Prior defenses (Autodefense, LLM self-defense, prefix-prompt, signed prompts, instruction/data separation) are compared narratively in a related-work table with their published numbers, never re-run.
key_result: Ablating the three modules on the 2,905-prompt set: no defense 63.06% accuracy (P 0.678 / R 0.450), OV only 79.28%, CAP only 84.68% (P 0.891 / R 0.779), CAP+OV 95.25% (P 0.938 / R 0.966), and CAP+OV+SFL after 10 epochs 97.83% (P 0.980 / R 0.975), cutting false negatives from 48 to 35. The headline claim is that layered contextual + output + adaptive defenses compose, not that any single module suffices.
technical_summary: Proposes the Prompt-Shield Framework (PSF), a three-module defense wrapped around a locally hosted Llama 3.2 API. Context-Aware Parsing embeds the incoming turn and the preceding three turns with bert-base-uncased, rejects inputs whose cosine relevance falls below 0.70, runs spaCy dependency parsing against a DisallowedIntents list, and applies an embedding-drift check intended to catch gradual multi-turn manipulation. Output Validation screens generated responses, and a Self-Feedback Loop periodically folds newly flagged patterns back into the intent blocklist and validation rules. Evaluates the five module combinations as a binary classification task over a self-assembled corpus of jailbreak-derived adversarial prompts and benign chatbot prompts. Reports classification accuracy rather than end-to-end attack success on the protected application, and compares only against its own ablations.
datasets_benchmarks: 2,905-prompt balanced set assembled by the authors: 1,405 adversarial prompts curated from the public verazuo/jailbreak_llms corpus (15,140 prompts harvested from Reddit and Discord, Dec 2022-Dec 2023) plus 1,500 benign prompts from a university-administration chatbot setting. No standard prompt-injection benchmark is used.

source_title: Secure Artificial Intelligence (SAI): A Dual-layer defence model against prompt injection and prompt poisoning attacks
baselines_compared: Undefended ChatGPT and undefended Gemini on the same two prompts. No prior defense is compared, and no ablation is performed.
key_result: Qualitative only: on two adversarial prompts, both ChatGPT and Gemini produced the harmful content (including code snippets) while SAI's guard model blocked both, identified as disguised keylogger requests. The only number in the paper is a secondhand claim that 'up to 30% of prompt-based manipulation attempts successfully bypass default ethical and safety constraints', attributed to prior work rather than measured here.
technical_summary: Proposes SAI (Secure Artificial Intelligence), a dual-layer architecture in which a specialized 'guard' LLM classifies each incoming prompt as safe or malicious before it reaches a primary response model, rejecting malicious ones outright. Describes a training regime for the guard model over datasets of known bypass tactics with incremental fine-tuning and error-sensitivity tuning to balance false positives, plus periodic red-team evaluation and patching. Validates only by demonstration: two crafted jailbreak prompts are shown bypassing ChatGPT and Gemini while being blocked by SAI. Provides no dataset, no metrics, no baseline defense comparison and no identification of the underlying models. The architecture is essentially the standard input-classifier/guard-model pattern presented under a new name.
datasets_benchmarks: None - no dataset. Evaluation consists of two hand-written jailbreak prompts (a fictional 'humans are extinct / Arevala species' framing requesting keylogger code, and a role-play survival scenario) shown as screenshots.

defense_name: SPML-IR specification-based image defense (two-stage input validation + prompt injection detection)
source_title: Defending Language Models Against Image-Based Prompt Attacks via User-Provided Specifications
baselines_compared: RQ4 compares the proposed specification-based approach against the natural alternative of captioning the image and running existing text-based prompt-injection detection on the description; RQ3 compares against relying on the MLLM's own robustness with no defense. Three backbones are compared against each other. No prior MLLM defense is run, as the authors claim none exists.
key_result: Detection of the seven malicious images degraded sharply with backbone capability: 100% for GPT-4-Vision, 42.8% for LLaVA-13B, and 0% for MiniGPT-4, supporting the authors' point that the guarding model must be at least as capable as the model it protects. In the input-validation stage GPT-4-Vision and LLaVA-13B caught all invalid inputs (LLaVA needing output post-processing) while MiniGPT-4 hallucinated and missed half.
technical_summary: Proposes a two-stage, specification-driven defense for multimodal chatbots against image-borne prompt injection, extending the authors' prior SPML domain-specific language from text to images. Stage one, input validation, has an MLLM fill an SPML-IR skeleton derived from the programmer's declared expected-image specification (e.g. 'Image content = Parking Sign, quality = in-focus, text clear and readable') and rejects images whose filled skeleton conflicts with the specification, shrinking the attack surface before the chatbot ever sees the input. Stage two compares the attacker's inferred intent, expressed in the same IR, against the chatbot's declared specification to flag injections that survive stage one. The design is deliberately content-invariant: it checks conformance to a declared specification rather than scanning for malicious patterns. Validation is a single-chatbot case study with seven attack images across three backbones, not a benchmark evaluation.
datasets_benchmarks: None public. A single hand-built case study around a 'Parking Pal' chatbot: seven malicious input images (readable overlaid text, translucent-overlay text, near-invisible text, authority-framed chat-bubble imagery, tiled large-font text) plus a small set of valid and irrelevant images for the input-validation test.

source_title: Protection of LLM Environment Using Prompt Security
baselines_compared: None - no baseline defense, no ablation across the four engines, and no comparison to any prior detector.
key_result: LPDS reports 96.85% overall detection accuracy on the 10,000-prompt set with an average scan time of 0.42 s. Note a self-inconsistency: the narrative says 6,997 of 7,000 malicious prompts were caught and 2,988 of 3,000 benign prompts passed, while the confusion matrix in Table 1 gives 6,847/162 and 153/2,838 - the two do not reconcile.
technical_summary: Proposes LPDS (LLM Prompt Detection System), a four-engine gateway that scans both the inputs and the outputs of an LLM deployment. The PII engine combines 124 regular expressions with a Korean/English NER model and pseudonymizes what it finds; a fine-tuned openllama-3b engine performs binary prompt-injection classification; a URL engine checks against URLhaus; and a malware engine checks against VirusTotal. Evaluates the combined system as binary classification over a self-assembled 10,000-prompt corpus derived from artificial data and ShareGPT, reporting accuracy and per-scan latency. Notable for placing detection on the output path as well as the input path and for explicit Korean-language PII coverage, but there is no ablation isolating the injection engine, no baseline, and the reported confusion matrix contradicts the narrative counts.
datasets_benchmarks: Author-constructed 10,000-prompt set (7,000 malicious/PII-bearing, 3,000 benign) built from artificially generated data plus ShareGPT and its Korean translation; the malicious half mixes prompt injection, jailbreaking, malicious-code generation, malicious-URL and PII-extraction prompts. Threat intelligence feeds: URLhaus for malicious URLs and VirusTotal for malware. No public benchmark.

defense_name: Chunk-based hash + embedding prompt injection detection scheme (with optional blockchain audit logging)
source_title: Privacy-Preserving Prompt Injection Detection for Smart Cloud-Deployed Large Language Models
baselines_compared: Full-Text Embedding Detection scheme; Window-based Hash Detection scheme
key_result: The proposed chunk-based hash+embedding detection scheme reaches F1 scores above 0.94 (up to ~0.96) across NONE/TEMPLATE/BOTH/QUESTION categories, outperforming full-text embedding detection and window-based hash detection baselines, while never storing plaintext user prompts.
technical_summary: Proposes a privacy-preserving prompt injection detection scheme for cloud-deployed LLMs that combines salted hash-based exact matching with sentence-embedding-based near-match detection over sliding-window chunks of user prompts, so raw plaintext is never persistently stored. Adds an optional blockchain logging layer (tested on the Sepolia testnet) for tamper-evident audit trails of flagged prompts. Benchmarks the scheme against full-text embedding detection and window-based hash detection on 2,000 synthetic test prompts spanning four injection templates, showing consistently higher F1 across similarity thresholds and window sizes. Concludes the approach balances detection accuracy with strict privacy requirements.
datasets_benchmarks: 2,000 synthetically constructed test prompts combining four injection templates ("Ignore previous instructions", "Information overload", "Repeated-token attack", "System mode") with 50 prohibited-scenario questions and randomly generated normal questions, classified into NONE/TEMPLATE/QUESTION/BOTH

source_title: A Novel GNN-based Approach for Detection of Prompt Injection Attacks
key_result: The proposed GNN-based classifier achieves 98.70% accuracy and F1=0.9799 on the Safe-Guard Prompt Injection Dataset, outperforming Logistic Regression (F1=0.9372), XGBoost (F1=0.9171), and Random Forest (F1=0.8629); 5-fold CV gives 98.45% average accuracy.
technical_summary: Proposes a Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based classifier for detecting prompt injection attacks that represents text as a graph (words/phrases as nodes) and integrates transformer-based (BERT) embeddings with sentiment features to capture local and global semantic relationships. Evaluates on the Safe-Guard Prompt Injection Dataset against Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost baselines using accuracy, F1, precision/recall, and 5-fold cross-validation. Achieves the best accuracy (98.70%) and F1 (0.9799) among all compared models, at the cost of higher training time. Discusses practical trade-offs between detection accuracy and computational efficiency for real-time deployment.
datasets_benchmarks: Safe-Guard Prompt Injection Dataset (Hugging Face, xTRam1), 80/20 train/validation split, 5-fold cross-validation

defense_name: Windowed HTML content filtering (128/64-token chunking + PromptGuard/DeBERTaV3 classification)
source_title: Disrupting Large Language Models with Hidden Prompt Injection Attacks Embedded in HTML Pages
baselines_compared: Unfiltered LLM responses (raw ASR per model) vs. filtered responses using DeBERTaV3-based chunk filtering and PromptGuard-based chunk filtering, at 128-token and 64-token window sizes
key_result: Baseline ASR on the DM-X dataset ranges from 0% (SmolLM:1.7b) to 60.7% average (Mistral-Nemo:12b); the proposed 128/64-token windowed pre-processing filter using PromptGuard or DeBERTaV3 reduces ASR on DM-20 to roughly 7-28% depending on model and tokenizer, a substantial reduction versus unfiltered baselines.
technical_summary: Constructs a benchmark dataset (DisruptiveMessages / DM-10/15/20) of HTML pages containing randomly placed hidden prompt injections designed to hijack an LLM's response to a fixed keyword, and evaluates attack success rate across 12 open- and closed-source LLMs. Proposes a pre-processing defense that chunks retrieved HTML into fixed-size (128- or 64-token) windows, classifies each chunk with off-the-shelf detectors (Meta Prompt-Guard or ProtectAI's DeBERTaV3-prompt-injection-v2), and filters out flagged chunks before re-feeding the cleaned content to the LLM. Shows the filtering substantially reduces ASR relative to unfiltered baselines across models and window sizes. Releases the dataset and experiment code on GitHub.
datasets_benchmarks: Self-constructed "DisruptiveMessages" (DM-10, DM-15, DM-20) dataset: 500 HTML pages sampled from an open-source corpus, with 10/15/20 randomly placed hidden prompt injections per page

source_title: Hybrid Constitutional Classifiers for Prompt Injection Defense
baselines_compared: LLaMA-2 13B classifier (input and output); rule-based keyword/heuristic filtering system (input and output)
key_result: The hybrid classifier achieves 96.97% input-detection accuracy and 78.79% output-detection accuracy with a 0.23% input false-positive rate, offering 67% lower latency than a LLaMA-2 13B classifier baseline (98.43% input accuracy but far higher latency) while outperforming a rule-based filter's accuracy (56.52% input accuracy) despite its speed advantage.
technical_summary: Proposes a Hybrid Constitutional Classifier system combining a lightweight DeBERTa-based input classifier (filtering adversarial prompts before they reach the LLM) with a small fine-tuned LLM (Mistral-7B) for output/response monitoring to catch unsafe completions in real time. Benchmarks the hybrid system against a LLaMA-2 13B classifier and a rule-based filter on HarmBench/jailbreak/synthetic datasets, achieving 96.97% input-detection accuracy and 78.79% output-detection accuracy with 67% lower latency than the LLaMA-2 13B baseline. Explores quantization (INT4) and knowledge distillation to further reduce latency with modest accuracy loss. Identifies output-classifier false-positive rate and dataset diversity as remaining limitations for high-volume deployment.
datasets_benchmarks: HarmBench; Jailbreak Dataset; synthetic and manually collected adversarial prompt dataset (~1M+ train examples across input/output classifier splits)

defense_name: Enterprise Secure AI Execution Engine (Zero-Trust AI Security Gateway)
source_title: Enterprise Secure AI Execution Engine: A Zero-Trust Security Gateway for Enterprise LLM Systems
baselines_compared: Baseline LLM deployment with no security enforcement layer (direct prompt processing, minimal content filtering)
key_result: The proposed Secure AI Execution Engine achieves 98.7% block accuracy and 99.3% tokenization accuracy with a 1.3% false-allow rate, versus 82%/75%/12% for an unsecured baseline LLM deployment, at a modest latency cost (18ms vs. 12ms).
technical_summary: Introduces the Enterprise Secure AI Execution Engine, a Zero-Trust AI Security Gateway that enforces input sanitization, Role-Based Access Control (RBAC), adversarial prompt detection, and deterministic tokenization of sensitive entities before prompts reach an enterprise LLM. Evaluates the gateway on a 300-prompt adversarial subset derived from the HackAPrompt benchmark across five attack categories under three RBAC roles. Reports 98.7% block accuracy and 99.3% tokenization accuracy versus 82%/75% for an unprotected baseline LLM deployment, with only a modest latency increase. Identifies usability trade-offs from default-deny policies and dependence on detection-model accuracy as open limitations.
datasets_benchmarks: 300-prompt adversarial subset derived from the HackAPrompt benchmark, spanning 5 attack categories (Credential Extraction, Role Escalation Attempts, Encoded Payload Injection, SQL-like Data Extraction, Internal Document Access Requests; 60 prompts each), tested under 3 RBAC roles (Admin, Employee, Intern)

defense_name: Prompt Injection Threat Analysis + LLM Output Risk Monitoring framework
source_title: A Novel Security Framework against Prompt Injection Attacks
baselines_compared: Each fine-tuned module compared against its own pre-fine-tuning (base pretrained model) performance as an ablation baseline; no comparison to alternative published defense frameworks
key_result: The fine-tuned multi-module framework achieves 93.65% overall accuracy on an integrated evaluation dataset spanning privacy leakage, malicious-prompt, and language-attack tasks, with per-task accuracy after fine-tuning ranging from 84.39% (context dependency verification) to 99.94% (unauthorized-language risk analysis) - a 2-5% improvement over pre-fine-tuning baselines for most tasks.
technical_summary: Proposes a two-part security framework combining "Prompt Injection Threat Analysis" (malicious-prompt, unauthorized-language, and privacy-disclosure detection modules) with "LLM Output Risk Monitoring" (context-dependency verification and malicious-code output detection) for defending LLMs against prompt injection. Fine-tunes existing pretrained models (BERT, XLM-RoBERTa, Prompt-Guard-86M, DeBERTa-v3, bge-m3-zeroshot) on public HuggingFace/GitHub datasets for privacy detection, language identification, and jailbreak classification. Reports per-module accuracy gains of 2-5% from fine-tuning and 93.65% overall accuracy on an integrated multi-threat evaluation dataset. Positions itself as more robust than traditional keyword/rule-based filtering, though it largely assembles and fine-tunes existing off-the-shelf detector models rather than introducing a fundamentally new detection algorithm.
datasets_benchmarks: privacy detection dataset (HuggingFace); language-identification dataset (HuggingFace); jailbreak-classification dataset (HuggingFace); Safety-Prompts (GitHub, thu-coai)

defense_name: ChatTEDU dual-LLM architecture (LLM-1 moderation gatekeeper + LLM-2 response generator)
source_title: Securing With Dual-LLM Architecture: ChatTEDU an Open Access Chatbot’s Defense
baselines_compared: None implemented directly - authors explicitly acknowledge the absence of a baseline method comparison on the same dataset and flag side-by-side benchmarking against standardized attack corpora as future work
key_result: The dual-LLM (LLM-1 moderation + LLM-2 generation) architecture blocked 100% of 180 identified real-world malicious attempts (prompt injection, jailbreak, spam/DoS, content manipulation) across 4,501 total interactions, with only a 0.28% false-positive rate and 18% latency overhead (1.2s added to a 6.7s baseline), sustaining 95% throughput under peak concurrent load.
technical_summary: Introduces ChatTEDU, a dual-LLM defense architecture for an open-access, multilingual RAG-based educational chatbot deployed at TED University. Separates content moderation (LLM-1, GPT-4 with few-shot prompt-engineered threat classification) from response generation (LLM-2, GPT-4), so the moderation model gates all input before the generation model ever processes it. Evaluated against 4,501 real-world production interactions (180 malicious) collected over a two-month deployment, achieving 100% detection of identified attacks with 0.28% false positives and only 18% latency overhead while sustaining 95% throughput under peak concurrent load. Acknowledges that no baseline defense was directly compared on the same dataset and recommends future standardized benchmarking.
datasets_benchmarks: Real-world production dataset of 4,501 unique interactions (180 malicious, 4,321 benign) collected during a two-month (July-August 2024) deployment at TED University; no external benchmark or baseline defense method used for direct comparison
